summary.text: The asteroid belt is a torus-shaped region centered on the Sun, roughly between the orbits of Jupiter and Mars.
It holds a great many solid, irregularly shaped bodies called asteroids, which on average are about a million kilometers apart.
It formed from planetesimals whose growth into a planet was disrupted by Mars and Jupiter, and 99.9% of its original mass was lost.

facts.label: Largest member
facts.value: Ceres, about 950 km across, the only dwarf planet in the belt

facts.label: Asteroid types
facts.value: Most are carbonaceous, silicate, or X-type

facts.label: Mass lost
facts.value: 99.9% of the original mass in the first 100 million years

items.prompt: Many uncrewed spacecraft have crossed the asteroid belt without incident. What does that say about the belt?

options.label: Its asteroids are all far too small to be any danger
Probes slip through gaps swept clear by Jupiter
Its material is so thinly spread that crossing is easy
A magnetic field around it pushes asteroids aside

items.explain: The asteroid material is so thinly distributed that spacecraft have traversed it without incident.

items.prompt: A planet never formed in the asteroid belt. What stopped it?

options.label: The Sun's heat boiled away the gas the planet needed
Pulls by Mars and Jupiter shattered colliding planetesimals
A planet formed there but was flung out of orbit later
There was never enough rock in that region to start one

items.explain: Gravitational perturbations from Mars and Jupiter disrupted accretion and shattered colliding planetesimals and most incipient protoplanets.

items.prompt: Astronomers expected to find a planet between Mars and Jupiter. What led them to expect one?

options.label: Telescopes had already shown a fuzzy disc there
Comets kept disappearing from that part of the sky
Uranus was seen to be pulled by something near Mars
A numerical pattern in planet orbits left a gap there

items.explain: The Titius-Bode pattern fit the known planets only if a missing planet sat between Mars and Jupiter, and Uranus's orbit matching it strengthened that belief.

items.prompt: Ceres and Pallas stayed points of light even under the highest magnification. How did that set them apart from the planets known then?

options.label: Planets of the time resolved into discs; they did not
Planets of the time twinkled; they shone steadily
Planets of the time moved fast; they stood still
Planets of the time looked red; they looked white

items.explain: Unlike the other known planets, Ceres and Pallas remained points of light instead of resolving into discs.

items.prompt: By the early 1850s astronomers dropped Ceres, Pallas, Juno and Vesta from the planet list. What pushed them to do so?

options.label: Telescopes showed that they were really just stars
Neptune's discovery proved that they were comets
Newly found objects kept piling up at a growing rate
They were found to circle Jupiter instead of the Sun

items.explain: New objects were found at an accelerating rate, which made counting them among the planets cumbersome.

items.prompt: At certain distances in the asteroid belt, asteroids get swept into other orbits. What causes that?

options.label: The Sun's magnetic field pushing asteroids away
Repeated crashes with comets from the Kuiper belt
Radiation from Mars burning the rock off asteroids
Jupiter's resonance sweeping them into other orbits

items.explain: Where an asteroid's period of revolution forms an orbital resonance with Jupiter, a Kirkwood gap occurs as they are swept into other orbits.
